memory_update.text: LEU should remain the reference public HALEU/enrichment benchmark for this node; later layers should focus on DOE task orders, NRC license continuity, and commercial scalability rather than theme popularity.
TLN is a direct regulated-baseload/data-center PPA asset-owner comp; useful as a demand validator for nuclear power monetization even though it is outside the preferred small/mid-cap discovery band.
UUUU belongs in the underfollowed lane as upstream domestic uranium exposure, but its HALEU relation is indirect and must be validated through contracts and fuel-cycle policy flow-through.
ASPI is a speculative shadow candidate for alternative enrichment/HALEU technology; require licensing, binding offtake, spin-out, and facility milestones before promotion to a higher-confidence lane.

This pass did not fully map US-listed nuclear instrumentation, valves, heat exchangers, testing/inspection, or licensing-support firms; those should be covered in a separate component/services Layer 1B pass.
LEU remains the direct public reference for U.S. HALEU enrichment exposure; use it as the benchmark for all other fuel-cycle candidates.
SILXY/Silex is a speculative-shadow candidate because OTCQX access and GLE ownership create potential fuel-cycle leverage, but commercialization, NRC licensing, and revenue timing remain unproven.
FLS is an underfollowed component candidate: nuclear-qualified pumps, valves, seals, and service may be a second-order bottleneck if nuclear projects accelerate.
FLR is an underfollowed EPC/execution-capacity candidate, but NuScale stake monetization and project-risk exposure must be checked before promoting beyond Layer 1.

Need a follow-up search for public suppliers of nuclear graphite, ASME N-stamp pressure vessels, steam generators, nuclear instrumentation, radiation monitoring, and non-destructive testing firms with U.S. listings.

SOLS should be retained for later layers as a hidden uranium-conversion chokepoint because the nuclear exposure is embedded inside a specialty-materials spin-off rather than a conventional uranium/miner label.
MIR should be tracked as a second-order nuclear compliance and instrumentation gate, especially if SMR, restart, and fuel-cycle facility activity creates measurable order growth.
ASPI belongs in speculative_shadow only until HALEU licensing, facility, offtake, and commercial-scale enrichment evidence improves.
Fuel-cycle nodes split into at least three public-market subnodes for later work: conversion, enrichment/HALEU, and radiation/compliance instrumentation.

Need a separate pass for listed nuclear pumps, valves, heat exchangers, specialty EPC subcontractors, and ASME/NQA-1 certified component suppliers; Flowserve surfaced as a possible but was excluded from this four-name cap.
LEU should remain the HALEU reference anchor for the nuclear-fuel-cycle node, but it is not the cleanest underfollowed discovery name because market attention around HALEU is already meaningful.

MIR is a promising underfollowed adjacent nuclear-instrumentation candidate: exposure is plausibly tied to reactor monitoring, radiation safety, licensing/compliance, SMR instrumentation, and nuclear-facility operations rather than uranium price beta.

GHM is a second-order component candidate with possible SMR, cryogenic, heat-transfer, turbomachinery, and naval nuclear propulsion relevance; survival in later layers depends on proving material nuclear/SMR backlog.
ASPI belongs only in the speculative_shadow lane until independent technical validation, licensing, financing, and commercial HALEU production milestones are verified.

For data-center nuclear power, the research map should separate regulated baseload demand validators from harder supply-chain constraints: HALEU/enrichment, conversion, reactor instrumentation, qualified heat-transfer components, nuclear QA/certification, and specialized EPC/licensing support.

Further searches should target US-listed nuclear valve, pump, heat-exchanger, inspection/testing, licensing-support, and EPC subcontractor names; many relevant suppliers may be private or buried inside diversified industrials.

node: Nuclear fuel cycle, HALEU enrichment, and regulated baseload supply for data-center power
summary: Combined focused Layer 1B searches: Layer 1B expands direct public-market exposure around nuclear fuel-cycle bottlenecks and regulated baseload supply for AI/data-center power. The strongest evidence sits in HALEU/enrichment and nuclear-backed PPA asset owners; upstream uranium and new enrichment technologies remain plausible but require stricter verification. This is research support only, not a trading recommendation. Layer 1B expansion found a narrow public-market universe around the nuclear fuel-cycle and regulated-baseload chokepoint. The strongest direct exposure is still Centrus Energy because HALEU enrichment is a core bottleneck for many advanced reactors. The underfollowed discovery lane adds Silex Systems via its OTCQX listing and majority ownership of Global Laser Enrichment, plus less-obvious component and execution bottleneck names Flowserve and Fluor. These are not recommendations; they are research candidates requiring verification of backlog, customer contracts, NRC milestones, and revenue sensitivity to nuclear/data-center demand. Layer 1B expands the node away from headline utilities and SMR developers toward fuel-cycle bottlenecks and nuclear-adjacent compliance gates. The highest-evidence reference name remains Centrus Energy for HALEU/enrichment.
